docs.title: CTRAIN
docs.text: CTRAIN is a unified, modular and comprehensive Python library for certified training and neural network verification. It provides implementations of state-of-the-art certified training methods through a consistent interface, facilitating their application, comparison and extension. Based on PyTorch and auto_LiRPA, CTRAIN integrates into existing machine learning workflows and supports configuring, training and formally evaluating neural networks.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
CTRAIN integrates multiple state-of-the-art certified training approaches, which are:

  • Interval Bound Propagation (IBP) (Gowal et al., 2018 with the improvements of Shi et al., 2021)
  • CROWN-IBP (Zhang et al., 2020)
  • SABR (Müller et al., 2023)
  • TAPS (Mao et al., 2023)
  • STAPS (combination of SABR and TAPS, Mao et al., 2023)
  • MTL-IBP, CC-IBP and Exp-IBP, the family of expressive losses combining adversarial and certified objectives (De Palma et al., 2024)
  • CC-Dist, combining CC-IBP with feature distillation from an adversarially trained teacher (De Palma, 2026)
  • IBP-R, augmenting adversarial training with an IBP-based regulariser (De Palma et al., 2022)
  • Gaussian loss smoothing, enabling training with tighter bounding methods through Randomized Gradient Smoothing (RGS) or Policy Gradients with Parameter-based Exploration (PGPE) (Balauca et al., 2025)
  • Set-based training, propagating zonotopes through the network to optimise reachable output enclosures (Koller et al., 2025)

These methods share implementations of bound propagation, loss calculation, adversarial attacks and regularisation. This modular design allows researchers to investigate new approaches by modifying individual components without having to reimplement existing baselines from scratch.

Beyond local robustness, CTRAIN supports training for general input-output properties, expressed as Boolean combinations of affine output constraints over input boxes. By formulating these properties through satisfaction margins, analogous to classification margins, CTRAIN enables adaptations of existing certified training methods to more general specifications, such as output-range constraints or relations between multiple predictions.

Furthermore, CTRAIN enables easy evaluation of the adversarial and certified robustness of a given neural network, using the following methods:

  • PGD (Madry et al., 2018)
  • AutoAttack, an ensemble of complementary adversarial attacks (Croce and Hein, 2020)
  • IBP (Gowal et al., 2018)
  • CROWN-IBP (Zhang et al., 2020)
  • CROWN (Zhang et al., 2018)
  • α-CROWN (Xu et al., 2021)
  • α,β-CROWN (Xu et al., 2021, Wang et al., 2021)
  • NeuralSAT (Duong et al., 2025), a complete neural network verification system based on the DPLL(T) framework

For incomplete verification, users can select a single method or apply methods adaptively in increasing order of computational cost. Complete verification first attempts to resolve inputs using incomplete methods and PGD before invoking α,β-CROWN or NeuralSAT. The evaluation functions can also be used independently of CTRAIN's training workflow to assess externally trained models.

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
CTRAIN has the goal of providing a unified, comprehensive, accessible and flexible framework for certified training. Key features include:

  • Standardised, modular and highly configurable implementations of popular and performant certified training methods based on the popular auto_LiRPA library
  • Unified and accessible interface through model wrappers
  • Based on PyTorch for easy integration into common machine learning pipelines
  • Native support for hyperparameter optimisation with preconfigured, method-specific search spaces, including single-objective optimisation using SMAC3 (Lindauer et al., 2022) and multi-objective optimisation using Optuna/BoTorch as proposed by Kaulen et al., 2026 (see below)
  • Training and verification for general input-output properties beyond local robustness
  • Comprehensive evaluation tools for adversarial and certified robustness
  • Support for both incomplete and complete verification methods, including the state-of-the-art complete verification systems α,β-CROWN and NeuralSAT
  • Detailed documentation with API reference, setup guide, and usage examples
  • Open-source with a permissive MIT license
  • Active development and maintenance by the Chair for Artificial Intelligence Methodology at RWTH Aachen University

docs.title: Installation and Quick Start
docs.text:
Install CTRAIN and its pinned Git dependencies (including auto_LiRPA):

pip install CTRAIN
ctrain-install-git-deps

For development, run these commands from a checkout of the CTRAIN repository:

git submodule update --init --recursive
pip install -e ".[dev]"
ctrain-install-git-deps

The dependency installer obtains the pinned versions of auto_LiRPA, onnx2pytorch and AutoAttack used by CTRAIN. Further setup instructions are provided in the installation guide.

Then, you can train and evaluate the standard CNN7 architecture proposed by Shi et al. on the CIFAR-10 dataset using IBP in a few lines of code:

from CTRAIN.model_definitions import CNN7_Shi
from CTRAIN.data_loaders import load_cifar10
from CTRAIN.model_wrappers import ShiIBPModelWrapper

train_loader, test_loader = load_cifar10(val_split=False)
in_shape = [3, 32, 32]

model = CNN7_Shi(in_shape=in_shape)
wrapped_model = ShiIBPModelWrapper(model=model, input_shape=in_shape, eps=2/255, num_epochs=160)

wrapped_model.train_model(train_loader)
wrapped_model.eval()
std_acc, cert_acc, adv_acc = wrapped_model.evaluate(test_loader)

The model wrapper encapsulates the PyTorch network and exposes training through train_model, evaluation through evaluate or evaluate_complete, and hyperparameter optimisation through hpo. To use another certified training method, choose the corresponding wrapper and its method-specific hyperparameters.

CTRAIN/
├── attacks/               # Adversarial attacks

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text: The documentation includes installation instructions, usage examples and an API reference.

docs.title: Getting started and guides
docs.text:
The following guides provide more detailed information about the different functionalities of CTRAIN:

  • Getting started: Installation instructions and a first runnable workflow.
  • Tutorials: Step-by-step examples of certified training, model evaluation, hyperparameter optimisation and training for general output properties.
  • Data and models: Data loading, input shapes, loader metadata and normalisation.
  • Training: Training schedules, shared configuration options and BatchNorm behaviour.
  • Checkpoints and model selection: Saving and restoring models, training state and validation-based model selection.
  • Hyperparameter optimisation: Running and resuming optimisation studies and selecting models from their Pareto fronts.
  • Evaluation and verification: Evaluating adversarial and certified robustness using attacks, incomplete certification and complete verification with α,β-CROWN and NeuralSAT.
  • General output properties: Defining and training against affine and Boolean output constraints over input boxes.
  • Troubleshooting: Common issues related to dependencies, model export and numerical computations.

docs.title: API Reference
docs.text:
The API reference provides detailed documentation of CTRAIN's classes, functions and configuration options. In particular, it covers the model wrappers, model definitions, data loaders and evaluation functions.

The reference documentation is generated directly from the source code and its docstrings. For explanations of how the different components interact and how to configure complete workflows, refer to the guides above.

docs.title: ICML 2026 Paper and Published Models
docs.text:
CTRAIN includes the code and result artifacts for the ICML 2026 paper “Rethinking Evaluation Paradigms in IBP-based Certified Training”, which compares certified-training methods through their natural-versus-certified accuracy Pareto fronts. The final, completely verified per-method fronts are available as published checkpoints.

Performance on clean data and certification of desired properties usually form a trade-off controlled by hyperparameter settings. CTRAIN implements the paper's multi-objective optimisation procedure through the wrappers' hpo method, returning a set of Pareto-optimal configurations from which users can select the model that best fits their application. See the hyperparameter optimisation tutorial for an example.

The published-model example shows how to inspect a published MTL-IBP front, download a model and evaluate it on CIFAR-10. The full paper code, results and reproduction instructions are provided in the paper artifacts.

docs.title: Implementation and Reproducibility
docs.text: CTRAIN standardises the shared components of certified training to facilitate comparison between methods. Reproducing a published experiment additionally requires its architecture, preprocessing, data splits, hyperparameters and evaluation protocol. The individual method pages linked in the overview describe the implemented objectives and differences from their source implementations.

docs.title: CC-Dist
docs.text:
CC-Dist extends CC-IBP with knowledge distillation from an adversarially trained teacher network, combining adversarial features and certified feature bounds to align the intermediate representations of the student with those of the teacher. Proposed by De Palma (2026), Learning Better Certified Models from Empirically-Robust Teachers, the method aims to improve the trade-off between natural accuracy and certified robustness by transferring knowledge from an empirically robust model.

In CTRAIN, CC-Dist is available through CCDistModelWrapper. It reuses the shared implementations of CC-IBP, PGD and IBP bounding, adding a feature-distillation term to the classification objective. The teacher is used during training; the resulting student can subsequently be evaluated and verified independently.

docs.title: Training Objective
docs.text:
CC-IBP combines adversarial classification margins with lower margin bounds obtained through IBP, before applying cross-entropy. CC-Dist additionally encourages the student's features to resemble those of the teacher. Here, features are the activations immediately before the final affine classifier.

For each training input, CTRAIN obtains the teacher's features on the unperturbed input, the student's features on a PGD adversarial example, and lower and upper IBP bounds on the student features. It then mixes each feature bound with the adversarial features using the same coefficient cc_ibp_alpha as the classification loss. For each feature coordinate, the distillation term takes the larger squared distance from the two mixed endpoints to the teacher feature. These distances are summed over coordinates and averaged over the batch.

The overall objective adds this distillation term, weighted by distillation_weight, to the CC-IBP loss. By default, distillation_weight=None selects the paper's coefficient of 5 / w, where w is the feature width. Setting distillation_weight=0 recovers the CC-IBP objective. The shared trainer additionally applies the configured Shi and L1 regularisers.

docs.title: Training with CTRAIN
docs.text:
In the following example, we train a CNN7 teacher and student on CIFAR-10 for robustness against ℓ∞ perturbations with radius ε = 2/255. First, we import the required functions and load the dataset using CTRAIN. Its loader supplies the normalisation metadata and input limits required for adversarial attacks and bound propagation.

from CTRAIN.data_loaders import load_cifar10
from CTRAIN.model_definitions import CNN7_Shi
from CTRAIN.model_wrappers import PGDModelWrapper, CCDistModelWrapper

input_shape = (3, 32, 32)
train_loader, test_loader = load_cifar10(batch_size=128, val_split=False)

docs.title: Training the Teacher
docs.text:
To obtain an empirically robust teacher, we wrap a CNN7 model with PGDModelWrapper and call train_model. This wrapper trains an ordinary PyTorch network using adversarial examples. By default, it uses SGD with momentum 0.9 and a triangular learning-rate schedule that increases from zero to 0.2 and then decreases to zero. Each training attack uses ten PGD steps with relative step size 0.25.

teacher = PGDModelWrapper(
    model=CNN7_Shi(in_shape=input_shape),
    input_shape=input_shape,
    eps=2 / 255,
    num_epochs=30,
    l1_reg_weight=1e-5,
    device="cuda",
)
teacher.train_model(train_loader)

An existing pretrained teacher can also be supplied. In that case, construct its native PyTorch architecture and load the corresponding weights before passing it to the student wrapper.

docs.title: Training the Student
docs.text:
Now, we construct a new CNN7 model and wrap it with CCDistModelWrapper. The teacher argument receives the trained PyTorch model, available through teacher.original_model. CTRAIN makes a private, frozen copy of its feature extractor, which supplies the target features throughout student training.

We configure one warm-up epoch using clean cross-entropy, followed by 80 ramp-up epochs during which the perturbation radius gradually increases to its target. The remaining epochs train at the full radius. Here, cc_ibp_alpha=0.01 controls the mixture of adversarial and IBP terms in both the classification and distillation losses.

student = CCDistModelWrapper(
    model=CNN7_Shi(in_shape=input_shape),
    input_shape=input_shape,
    eps=2 / 255,
    num_epochs=160,
    teacher=teacher.original_model,
    cc_ibp_alpha=0.01,
    warm_up_epochs=1,
    ramp_up_epochs=80,
    lr_decay_kwargs={"milestones": (120, 140), "gamma": 0.2},
    pgd_steps=8,
    pgd_alpha=0.25,
    pgd_eps_factor=2.1,
    l1_reg_weight=3e-6,
    device="cuda",
)
student.train_model(train_loader)

The pgd_eps_factor enlarges the input region searched by PGD, while IBP still uses the nominal training region. Training schedules, regularisation and the shared BatchNorm and ReLU-retention options are described in the training guide.

Without a validation loader, train_model returns the final weights. To select weights using validation data, load a separate validation split and pass it through val_loader. CC-Dist selects the model with the smallest robust validation data loss after ramp-up.

docs.title: Evaluating the Student
docs.text:
Finally, we set the student to evaluation mode and assess its natural, certified and adversarial accuracy using the common evaluation interface. The following call uses CROWN for incomplete verification and PGD for adversarial evaluation:

student.eval()
std_acc, cert_acc, adv_acc = student.evaluate(test_loader, eval_method="CROWN")

Complete verification can be invoked through student.evaluate_complete, using α,β-CROWN or NeuralSAT. Both forms of certification concern the student over the full nominal input box; the teacher is excluded from the verified network. See the evaluation guide for the available methods, solver settings and interpretation of results.

docs.title: Model Requirements and Training Behaviour
docs.text:
For CC-Dist, both teacher and student must be sequential classifiers ending in a Linear layer, with matching feature widths and class counts. CTRAIN accepts native torch.nn.Sequential models and model definitions exposing their sequential computation through .layers, including CNN7_Shi. Supported feature layers comprise convolutions, linear layers, BatchNorm, ReLU, Flatten and Identity. Although PGDModelWrapper can train more general networks, including residual architectures, the CC-Dist feature extractor currently requires this sequential structure.

During training, the frozen teacher evaluates clean inputs in evaluation mode. Student attacks also run in evaluation mode, while the loss on the resulting adversarial examples is computed in training mode. After warm-up, the student uses the adversarial batch statistics for both feature extraction and IBP. Thus, models with BatchNorm require the LiRPA settings forward_before_compute_bounds=False and bn.mode="forward", which are the defaults. Incompatible settings are rejected before training.

The teacher's parameters are excluded from the student's optimiser, saved inference weights and exported model. When resuming student training, supply the same pretrained teacher and training options again. Teacher training can separately be resumed through PGDModelWrapper.resume_from_checkpoint, which restores its native weights, optimiser and learning-rate scheduler. Further details are provided in the checkpoint guide.

docs.title: Hyperparameter Optimisation
docs.text:
CC-Dist supports the shared hyperparameter optimisation interface, including multi-objective searches over natural and certified validation accuracy. Train the teacher on the training partition and reserve separate validation data for the search. The teacher remains fixed across trials.

CTRAIN reuses the CC-IBP search space and additionally searches cc_dist:distillation_weight logarithmically over [0.1 / w, 50 / w], with default 5 / w. This search range is a CTRAIN configuration choice around the paper's fixed coefficient. To change its default, pass defaults={"distillation_weight": value} to hpo, choosing a value within that range. Run the no-distillation control separately with distillation_weight=0.

docs.title: Implementation and API Reference
docs.text:
CTRAIN provides an independent implementation of Algorithm 1 and equations (8)–(9) of the CC-Dist paper. The example above demonstrates its use through the library; reproducing reported accuracies additionally requires matching the experiment's data, training and verification protocols.

The API reference documents the CC-Dist wrapper, trainer and distillation loss, as well as the PGD teacher wrapper and adversarial trainer.

docs.title: Complete Verification
docs.text:
To establish whether a trained network satisfies a desired property, CTRAIN provides interfaces to the complete verification systems α,β-CROWN and NeuralSAT. These systems combine bound computations with search, allowing them to resolve properties that remain undecided by inexpensive incomplete methods. A finite computational budget can still leave a query unresolved.

Both backends are available through the common evaluate_complete method. CTRAIN prepares the network and specifications, performs initial screening, invokes the selected verifier and records the results. This workflow can also be used for models trained outside CTRAIN, provided their architecture and preprocessing are reconstructed correctly.

docs.title: Verification Workflow
docs.text:
For local robustness, the verification property requires the network to predict the correct class throughout a perturbation box around each evaluated input. CTRAIN constructs these boxes using the configured eps, loader normalisation metadata and input limits.

The evaluator first identifies clean classification errors, then applies IBP and CROWN to the remaining inputs and uses PGD to search for adversarial examples. Only unresolved queries are passed to the complete backend. Thus, inputs that can be certified or falsified cheaply do not require a full solver invocation.

To interface with the complete backends, CTRAIN exports the network to ONNX and writes input regions and output constraints in VNNLIB format. The selected verifier receives these files for the unresolved queries. Export includes numerical comparisons with the internal model representation. Verification concerns the exported graph under the solver's numerical assumptions; these comparisons are checks on sampled inputs rather than a proof of equivalence over the whole input region.

docs.title: Preparing the Model
docs.text:
The following example evaluates the MNIST model saved as mnist_ibp.pt in the getting-started guide. First, we load the test data and recreate the architecture and wrapper configuration used for training.

import torch

from CTRAIN.data_loaders import load_mnist
from CTRAIN.model_definitions import CNN7_Shi
from CTRAIN.model_wrappers import ShiIBPModelWrapper

device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")
input_shape = (1, 28, 28)
train_loader, test_loader = load_mnist(
    batch_size=128, val_split=False, data_root="./data", workers=0
)

wrapped_model = ShiIBPModelWrapper(
    model=CNN7_Shi(in_shape=input_shape, n_classes=10),
    input_shape=input_shape,
    eps=0.1,
    num_epochs=70,
    warm_up_epochs=1,
    ramp_up_epochs=40,
    lr_decay_kwargs={"milestones": (50, 60), "gamma": 0.2},
    device=device,
)
wrapped_model.load_state_dict(
    torch.load("mnist_ibp.pt", map_location=device, weights_only=True)
)
wrapped_model.eval()

The saved file contains wrapper inference weights, so it is loaded after constructing the bounded model. Native PyTorch weights are instead loaded into the architecture before wrapping. In either case, the architecture, preprocessing, class count and perturbation radius must match the intended experiment; the model evaluation tutorial explains the supported checkpoint formats.

Complete verification requires a sequential evaluation loader with a defined batch size and drop_last=False, using evaluation transforms. CTRAIN's test loaders provide this configuration. The shared evaluator captures the transformed inputs so that screening and solver calls use the same images and input regions.

docs.title: abCROWN
docs.text:
α,β-CROWN combines optimised linear-relaxation bounds with branch-and-bound search. Select it through engine="abcrown", which is also the default. Here, we evaluate the first ten test images with a solver budget of 300 seconds per unresolved input.

Choose a fresh results_path for a new experiment. To continue an existing evaluation, use the warm-start options described below.

std_acc, cert_acc, adv_acc = wrapped_model.evaluate_complete(
    test_loader,
    engine="abcrown",
    test_samples=10,
    timeout=300,
    abcrown_batch_size=128,
    results_path="./verification/mnist_abcrown",
)

The abcrown_batch_size controls the solver's batch size and can be reduced when memory is limited. Additional backend settings can be supplied as a nested abcrown_config_dict, following the upstream configuration documentation. The no_cores argument controls parallel MIP solvers when that functionality is enabled. The bundled adapter selects the available compute device automatically.

docs.title: NeuralSAT
docs.text:
NeuralSAT combines neural network abstraction with DPLL(T)-based search. To evaluate the same model and input prefix with this backend, select engine="neuralsat" and use a separate result directory:

std_acc, cert_acc, adv_acc = wrapped_model.evaluate_complete(
    test_loader,
    engine="neuralsat",
    test_samples=10,
    timeout=300,
    neuralsat_batch_size=1000,
    results_path="./verification/mnist_neuralsat",
)

The neuralsat_batch_size controls the solver's maximum parallel branches. NeuralSAT uses the wrapper's CPU or CUDA device. Its adapter launches the solver in a subprocess and includes process startup in the timeout. An abcrown_config_dict cannot be used with this backend.

The timeout applies to each solver query, rather than to the complete evaluation. The total running time also includes screening, export and setup, and depends on how many inputs require complete verification.

docs.title: Interpreting Results
docs.text:
Both backends return the tuple (standard_accuracy, certified_accuracy, adversarial_accuracy), with values expressed as fractions:

print(f"Standard accuracy: {std_acc:.2%}")
print(f"Certified accuracy: {cert_acc:.2%}")
print(f"Adversarial accuracy: {adv_acc:.2%}")

Certified accuracy counts inputs whose robustness has been established. Adversarial accuracy counts inputs for which no violation has been found, including unresolved cases. These provide lower and upper bounds, respectively, on robust accuracy for the evaluated inputs. Matching bounds indicate that every input in the evaluated set has been resolved.

CTRAIN additionally saves per-input records under results_path/results_filename, where results_filename defaults to results.json. Each record includes a result, the method that produced it and the accumulated running time. The result statuses have the following meanings:

Result Meaning "unsat" The counterexample query is unsatisfiable; the property is certified. "sat" A clean error, adversarial attack or solver result reports a property violation. "timeout" The query exhausted its computational budget and remains unresolved. "unknown" or None The query remains unresolved, including unsuccessful solver executions.

The method field distinguishes screening results from backend results. Logs are saved under abCROWN_logs or neuralsat_logs within the result directory. Inspect these records and logs when investigating unresolved queries or solver-reported counterexamples; see the evaluation guide for numerical and witness semantics.

docs.title: Resuming and Splitting Evaluations
docs.text:
Set warm_start=True to reuse an existing result file. Keep the model, loader order, preprocessing, radius, engine and evaluated input prefix unchanged. A sidecar file, results.json.manifest.json by default, binds the saved records to the exported model, captured inputs, labels and perturbation region. Mismatches and legacy result files without a manifest are rejected.

The identity manifest does not capture every solver setting. Use a new result directory when changing budgets or backend configuration. Cached timeout records are retained on a warm start, so retrying them with a larger budget also requires a fresh evaluation.

For longer runs, start_idx and end_idx select a half-open slice of the prefix defined by test_samples, retaining global input indices in the result file. Keep test_samples fixed when processing several chunks of the same evaluation. The certified and adversarial accuracies returned for a chunk refer to that slice; the wrapper's standard accuracy is still computed over the full test_samples prefix. Use the per-input records when aggregating chunk results.

docs.title: Backend Setup
docs.text:
Install CTRAIN and its pinned Git dependencies as described in the installation guide. Both complete backends are bundled with the library; their source provenance and licences are retained in CTRAIN/verification_systems.

NeuralSAT's bundled runtime requires Python 3.10 or newer and runs with the active interpreter by default. Its own auto_LiRPA and onnx2pytorch forks are isolated in the solver subprocess. Keep CTRAIN's training dependencies in place; the bundled runtime does not require installing NeuralSAT's upstream requirements over them. Its licence probe disables optional MIP functionality when no usable Gurobi licence is available.

To run NeuralSAT from a separate checkout or Python environment, provide an argument-list prefix through neuralsat_command, for example ['/path/venv/bin/python', '/path/neuralsat/src/main.py']. This changes the solver process while retaining CTRAIN's shared export, screening and result handling.

docs.title: Implementation and API Reference
docs.text:
The common evaluator handles ONNX export, VNNLIB generation, screening, result persistence and backend dispatch. abCROWN and NeuralSAT adapters handle their respective invocation and status reporting. General output specifications use the separate property-certification interface.

The API reference documents the evaluation functions, wrapper interface, abCROWN integration and NeuralSAT integration. The model evaluation tutorial provides an interactive workflow with optional solver calls.

docs.title: CROWN-IBP
docs.text:
CROWN-IBP combines efficient interval propagation with tighter backward linear-relaxation bounds. Proposed by Zhang et al. (2020), Towards Stable and Efficient Training of Verifiably Robust Neural Networks, it uses IBP to obtain intermediate activation bounds and CROWN to bound the classification margins. This provides a way to stabilise the early stages of training, when IBP bounds can be particularly loose.

CTRAIN provides CROWN-IBP through CrownIBPModelWrapper. It shares the scheduling, initialisation, regularisation and evaluation infrastructure of Shi-style IBP training, adding controls for the mixture of bound estimates and optional loss fusion.

docs.title: Training Objective
docs.text:
CROWN-IBP first propagates the input box forward using IBP to obtain intermediate bounds. These intervals constrain a backward CROWN pass that computes lower bounds on the differences between the correct-class logit and competing logits.

In the explicit-margin path, selected through loss_fusion=False, CTRAIN interpolates between the IBP and CROWN-IBP lower margin bounds:

b_mixed = beta * b_CROWN_IBP + (1 - beta) * b_IBP

Cross-entropy is then computed from the mixed margins. The start_beta and end_beta arguments control the initial and final CROWN-IBP contribution, defaulting to 1 and 0. Thus, the default schedule gradually shifts from CROWN-IBP towards IBP as the perturbation radius increases.

The trainer separately supports a clean-loss mixing coefficient:

L_train = kappa * L_clean + (1 - kappa) * L_certified

The start_kappa and end_kappa arguments both default to zero, so positive-radius training uses the certified classification objective. At zero radius, training uses clean cross-entropy. Shi and L1 regularisation are configured separately.

docs.title: Training with CTRAIN
docs.text:
In the following example, we train CNN7 on CIFAR-10 for robustness against ℓ∞ perturbations with radius ε = 2/255. First, we import the required functions, load the dataset and construct the network.

from CTRAIN.data_loaders import load_cifar10
from CTRAIN.model_definitions import CNN7_Shi
from CTRAIN.model_wrappers import CrownIBPModelWrapper

input_shape = (3, 32, 32)
train_loader, test_loader = load_cifar10(batch_size=128, val_split=False)
model = CNN7_Shi(in_shape=input_shape)

Now, we configure the wrapper with one warm-up epoch and 80 ramp-up epochs. During ramp-up, the perturbation radius increases and the bound mixture transitions from its initial to final coefficient. Here, we explicitly select the margin-based loss computation described above.

wrapped_model = CrownIBPModelWrapper(
    model=model,
    input_shape=input_shape,
    eps=2 / 255,
    num_epochs=160,
    warm_up_epochs=1,
    ramp_up_epochs=80,
    start_beta=1.0,
    end_beta=0.0,
    loss_fusion=False,
    lr_decay_kwargs={"milestones": (120, 140), "gamma": 0.2},
    device="cuda",
)
wrapped_model.train_model(train_loader)

The loader supplies input limits and normalisation metadata, so the radius is specified in raw pixel units. The wrapper delegates the epoch loop and schedules to the library trainer; changing the training objective does not require a separate reproduction script.

docs.title: Evaluating the Model
docs.text:
Finally, we set the model to evaluation mode and assess its natural, certified and adversarial accuracy. This call uses CROWN-IBP for certification and PGD for adversarial evaluation:

wrapped_model.eval()
std_acc, cert_acc, adv_acc = wrapped_model.evaluate(
    test_loader, eval_method="CROWN-IBP"
)

Other incomplete methods can be selected through eval_method, and complete verification is available through evaluate_complete. Evaluation uses the ordinary model and the full nominal input region, independently of the training bound mixture or loss-fusion graph.

docs.title: Loss Fusion
docs.text:
The wrapper defaults to loss_fusion=True. In this mode, auto_LiRPA includes the cross-entropy computation in a separate bounded graph, allowing the trainer to bound the fused loss directly and reduce the memory cost of the computation. The trainer supplies the current inputs and labels to this graph before computing its bounds.

The fused graph has its own BatchNorm buffers. CTRAIN synchronises the relevant buffers with the ordinary model and supports population recalibration before selection and checkpointing. Its optimiser and learning-rate scheduler operate on the fused training parameters.

The fused training path currently reports an unavailable (NaN) certified-accuracy statistic because it does not return the per-class margin bounds used for that metric. This statistic should be obtained separately through the ordinary evaluation API. The explicit-margin path in the example makes the bound mixture directly accessible without changing the evaluation interface.

docs.title: Training Behaviour and Configuration
docs.text:
The trainer applies Shi initialisation when starting from epoch zero and supports the shared Shi and L1 regularisers. The shi_reg_weight and shi_reg_decay options control warm-up/ramp-up regularisation, while l1_reg_weight controls the L1 contribution. These additions should be considered when comparing a configuration with the original CROWN-IBP experiments.

The train_eps_factor scales the target training radius, while evaluation continues to use the nominal eps. Optional population BatchNorm recalibration is available through population_bn. Both the beta and kappa endpoints must lie in [0, 1]. Further shared options are described in the training guide.

Without a validation loader, train_model returns the final weights. Supplying val_loader enables selection after ramp-up by the smallest configured validation data loss at the fixed evaluation radius, using the selected bound mixture and loss-fusion setting. Trajectory checkpoints retain the training and selection state; the checkpoint guide explains saving and resumption.

docs.title: Hyperparameter Optimisation
docs.text:
CROWN-IBP supports the shared hyperparameter optimisation interface, including multi-objective searches over natural and certified validation accuracy. Its search space includes the shared training parameters, clean-loss coefficients and final beta value, with the initial beta fixed to one. The chosen loss-fusion and population BatchNorm settings are retained when constructing trial wrappers.

Reserve separate validation data for the search and evaluate the selected model on the test split. The hyperparameter optimisation tutorial demonstrates this workflow.

docs.title: Implementation and API Reference
docs.text:
CrownIBPModelWrapper configures crown_ibp_train_model, while the loss function obtains the IBP and CROWN-IBP bounds through auto_LiRPA. The example demonstrates the library workflow; source-specific architectures, schedules, loss-fusion behaviour and verification protocols must be matched before drawing reproduction conclusions.

The API reference documents the CROWN-IBP wrapper, trainer, loss and bound computations.

docs.title: Expressive Losses
docs.text:
The family of expressive losses combines adversarial and certified training through convex combinations. Proposed by De Palma et al. (2024), Expressive Losses for Verified Robustness via Convex Combinations, these methods use a single coefficient to control the contribution of adversarial examples and IBP bounds to the training objective. This allows users to explore different trade-offs between natural accuracy and certified robustness.

CTRAIN provides three representatives of this family: MTL-IBP, CC-IBP and Exp-IBP. They share implementations of PGD, IBP bounding and the training procedure, while differing in how they combine the adversarial and certified components. Each method is available through a separate model wrapper with the common training, evaluation and hyperparameter optimisation interface.

docs.title: Training Objectives
docs.text:
For each training input, the methods obtain an adversarial example using PGD and lower bounds on the classification margins using IBP. A classification margin is the difference between the logit of the correct class and that of a competing class. Positive margins for every competing class indicate correct classification.

Let L_adv denote the batch-mean cross-entropy on the adversarial examples and L_IBP the corresponding loss computed from IBP margin bounds. The three methods combine these quantities as follows.

docs.title: MTL-IBP
docs.text:
MTL-IBP takes a weighted arithmetic mean of the two losses:

L_MTL = alpha * L_IBP + (1 - alpha) * L_adv

Thus, its coefficient directly determines the relative weight of the adversarial and IBP classification losses in the objective.

docs.title: CC-IBP
docs.text:
CC-IBP forms the convex combination before applying cross-entropy. Let a denote the margins at the adversarial examples and b the IBP lower margin bounds. The mixed margins are:

mixed_margins = alpha * b + (1 - alpha) * a

Cross-entropy is then evaluated on these mixed margins and averaged over the batch. The combination therefore takes place at the level of classification margins, coupling the two components before computing the loss. CC-Dist extends this objective with feature distillation from an adversarially trained teacher.

docs.title: Exp-IBP
docs.text:
Exp-IBP combines the losses geometrically, which is equivalent to taking a convex combination of their logarithms:

L_Exp = L_IBP ** alpha * L_adv ** (1 - alpha)

CTRAIN combines the two batch-mean losses, following the authors' implementation. It evaluates this expression in log space, handling zero losses to keep the computation and its gradients well defined.

For all three objectives, alpha=0 recovers the adversarial classification loss and alpha=1 recovers the IBP classification loss. Configured regularisation still applies at these endpoints. The coefficient must lie in [0, 1] and defaults to 0.5. Since the combination differs between methods, the same coefficient need not yield the same natural–certified accuracy trade-off.

docs.title: Training with CTRAIN
docs.text:
In the following example, we train the CNN7 architecture proposed by Shi et al. on CIFAR-10 using MTL-IBP, for robustness against ℓ∞ perturbations with radius ε = 2/255. First, we import the required functions, load the dataset and define the network.

from CTRAIN.data_loaders import load_cifar10
from CTRAIN.model_definitions import CNN7_Shi
from CTRAIN.model_wrappers import MTLIBPModelWrapper

input_shape = (3, 32, 32)
train_loader, test_loader = load_cifar10(batch_size=128, val_split=False)
model = CNN7_Shi(in_shape=input_shape)

Now, we wrap the network with MTLIBPModelWrapper and configure the training process. We use one warm-up epoch on clean cross-entropy, followed by 80 ramp-up epochs during which the perturbation radius gradually increases to its target. The remaining epochs train at the full radius. Here, mtl_ibp_alpha=0.004 gives the adversarial loss most of the weight, while retaining an IBP component.

wrapped_model = MTLIBPModelWrapper(
    model=model,
    input_shape=input_shape,
    eps=2 / 255,
    num_epochs=160,
    mtl_ibp_alpha=0.004,
    warm_up_epochs=1,
    ramp_up_epochs=80,
    lr_decay_kwargs={"milestones": (120, 140), "gamma": 0.2},
    pgd_steps=8,
    pgd_alpha=0.25,
    pgd_eps_factor=2.1,
    l1_reg_weight=3e-6,
    device="cuda",
)
wrapped_model.train_model(train_loader)

To use CC-IBP or Exp-IBP, import the corresponding wrapper and replace the coefficient argument as shown below. The other training options have the same meaning across the three wrappers.

Method Model wrapper Coefficient argument MTL-IBP MTLIBPModelWrapper mtl_ibp_alpha CC-IBP CCIBPModelWrapper cc_ibp_alpha Exp-IBP ExpIBPModelWrapper exp_ibp_alpha

The coefficient should be chosen for the method and task of interest. The hyperparameter optimisation interface can be used to investigate its effect alongside the other training parameters.

docs.title: Evaluating the Model
docs.text:
Finally, we set the model to evaluation mode and assess its natural, certified and adversarial accuracy. The following call uses CROWN for incomplete verification and PGD for adversarial evaluation:

wrapped_model.eval()
std_acc, cert_acc, adv_acc = wrapped_model.evaluate(test_loader, eval_method="CROWN")

Complete verification is available through wrapped_model.evaluate_complete, using α,β-CROWN or NeuralSAT. Certification evaluates the model over the full nominal input box using sound bounds. The mixed training objective itself is a surrogate for learning robustness; certification is performed separately through the evaluation interfaces.

docs.title: Training Behaviour and Configuration
docs.text:
The three wrappers delegate to the shared expressive trainer, which owns initialisation, schedules, Shi and L1 regularisation, checkpointing and model selection. During training, PGD searches run in evaluation mode, while the loss on the resulting adversarial examples is computed in training mode. This preserves CTRAIN's chosen BatchNorm policy across the three methods.

The pgd_steps, pgd_alpha and pgd_restarts options configure the training attack. In the example, pgd_eps_factor=2.1 widens the PGD search region without changing the nominal IBP region. Evaluation attacks have their own settings. The shared options also include optional population BatchNorm recalibration through population_bn and training-only ReLU shrinkage through relu_upper_retention known as ReLU shrinking employed in SABR. See the training guide for these options and their defaults.

Without a validation loader, train_model returns the final weights. To select a model using validation data, load a separate validation split and pass it through val_loader. Selection then uses the smallest robust validation data loss after ramp-up, computed with the chosen expressive objective at the evaluation radius. Trajectory checkpoints retain the model, optimiser, learning-rate scheduler and selection state; the checkpoint guide explains saving and resumption.

docs.title: Hyperparameter Optimisation
docs.text:
All three wrappers support the common hpo method, which searches for Pareto-optimal trade-offs between natural and certified validation accuracy. Reserve separate validation data for this search and use the test split to assess the selected model. The HPO guide explains the available samplers, budgets and model-selection workflow.

The method-specific search space includes the mixing coefficient, PGD step count, relative step size and search-range factor, alongside the shared training hyperparameters. CTRAIN searches the coefficient logarithmically over [0.001, 0.5]; direct wrapper construction accepts the full interval [0, 1]. Configuration keys use the method name as a prefix, such as mtl_ibp:mtl_ibp_alpha, cc_ibp:cc_ibp_alpha and exp_ibp:exp_ibp_alpha.

docs.title: Implementation and API Reference
docs.text:
The objectives follow the Expressive Losses paper and the authors' training implementation. CTRAIN provides separate wrappers and loss functions for the three methods, reusing the common attack and bound computations. Lower-level loss calls that request bounds return the underlying IBP margin bounds; CC-IBP's mixed margins belong to its training objective.

The example above demonstrates the library workflow. Reproducing reported accuracies additionally requires matching the experiment's architecture, preprocessing, data splits, training configuration and verification protocol.

The API reference documents the shared wrapper, expressive trainer and loss functions. Method-specific training entry points are documented for MTL-IBP, CC-IBP and Exp-IBP.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: CTRAIN provides model wrappers that encapsulate ordinary PyTorch networks and expose certified training, evaluation and hyperparameter optimisation through a consistent interface. In this guide, we install the library and train a first model, following the same workflow used throughout CTRAIN: load a dataset, define a neural network, wrap it with a training method, and evaluate the resulting model.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
First, install CTRAIN in the Python environment in which you intend to run your experiments:

python -m pip install CTRAIN
ctrain-install-git-deps

The second command installs the pinned Git-hosted dependencies used by CTRAIN, including auto_LiRPA, onnx2pytorch and AutoAttack, and requires network access. If you use Jupyter, select the same Python environment as the notebook kernel.

For development, run the following commands from the root of a CTRAIN repository checkout. The editable installation allows changes to the library's source code to be used directly and includes the testing and documentation tools.

git submodule update --init --recursive
python -m pip install -e ".[dev]"
ctrain-install-git-deps

The reference CPU test environment uses Python 3.11, PyTorch 2.3.1 and torchvision 0.18.1. Your PyTorch and torchvision installations should match each other and the intended CPU or CUDA environment. The optional NeuralSAT backend requires Python 3.10 or newer. See dependency troubleshooting for help with installation or import errors.

docs.title: Certified Training with CTRAIN
docs.text: In the following example, we train the CNN7 architecture proposed by Shi et al. on MNIST using IBP with Shi-style improvements. We want the network to be certifiably robust against ℓ∞ perturbations with radius ε = 0.1 around its inputs. This example trains on the real MNIST dataset; a CUDA GPU is recommended for the full training run.

docs.title: Loading Data and Defining the Model
docs.text:
First, we import PyTorch and the required functions from CTRAIN:

import torch

from CTRAIN.data_loaders import load_mnist
from CTRAIN.model_definitions import CNN7_Shi
from CTRAIN.model_wrappers import ShiIBPModelWrapper

Now, we load MNIST and construct the network. Each input is a single-channel image of size 28 × 28 pixels, and the model predicts one of ten digit classes. The device is selected according to whether CUDA is available.

device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")
input_shape = (1, 28, 28)

train_loader, test_loader = load_mnist(
    batch_size=128,
    val_split=False,
    data_root="./data",
)
model = CNN7_Shi(in_shape=input_shape, n_classes=10)

The loader downloads missing MNIST data to data_root by default. It also supplies input limits and normalisation metadata, which CTRAIN uses to construct perturbation regions. Thus, eps=0.1 is specified in raw pixel units even though the loader normalises the images. Further details on datasets, custom loaders and normalisation are provided in the data and models guide.

docs.title: Configuring and Training the Wrapper
docs.text:
To train the network certifiably, we wrap it with ShiIBPModelWrapper. Under the hood, the wrapper converts the PyTorch model into a bounded LiRPA graph and passes the training configuration to the library's trainer.

We configure 70 training epochs, including one warm-up epoch on clean cross-entropy and 40 ramp-up epochs during which the perturbation radius gradually increases to its target. Training then continues at the full radius. The learning rate is reduced by a factor of 0.2 at epochs 50 and 60.

wrapped_model = ShiIBPModelWrapper(
    model=model,
    input_shape=input_shape,
    eps=0.1,
    num_epochs=70,
    warm_up_epochs=1,
    ramp_up_epochs=40,
    lr_decay_kwargs={"milestones": (50, 60), "gamma": 0.2},
    device=device,
)

We initiate training by calling the wrapper's train_model method:

wrapped_model.train_model(train_loader)

With the loaders used here, training returns the final weights. To select a model using validation data, load MNIST with val_split=True, which returns training, validation and test loaders, and pass the validation loader through val_loader. The training guide explains schedules, regularisation and shared configuration options.

docs.title: Evaluating the Model
docs.text:
Finally, we set the model to evaluation mode and assess its natural, certified and adversarial accuracy. Here, we use IBP for certification and PGD for adversarial evaluation on the first 1,000 test images:

wrapped_model.eval()
std_acc, cert_acc, adv_acc = wrapped_model.evaluate(
    test_loader,
    test_samples=1_000,
    eval_method="IBP",
)

print(f"Standard accuracy: {std_acc:.2%}")
print(f"Certified accuracy: {cert_acc:.2%}")
print(f"Adversarial accuracy: {adv_acc:.2%}")

The returned values are fractions, displayed here as percentages. Certified accuracy measures the proportion of evaluated inputs for which robustness is established throughout the perturbation region. Adversarial accuracy measures the proportion that remain correctly classified after the PGD search. These provide lower and upper bounds, respectively, on robust accuracy for the evaluated samples.

CTRAIN also supports tighter incomplete verification methods and complete verification through α,β-CROWN and NeuralSAT. See the evaluation guide and model evaluation tutorial for these workflows.

docs.title: Saving the Model
docs.text:
We can save the trained wrapper's inference weights using the standard PyTorch interface:

torch.save(wrapped_model.state_dict(), "mnist_ibp.pt")

To use these weights in a later session, recreate the same architecture and wrapper configuration, then load the saved state dictionary:

wrapped_model.load_state_dict(
    torch.load("mnist_ibp.pt", map_location=device, weights_only=True)
)
wrapped_model.eval()

Keep the architecture, input normalisation and perturbation radius alongside the weights. To resume training with its optimiser and learning-rate scheduler, use trajectory checkpoints instead; the checkpoint guide explains how to configure saving and restoration.

docs.title: Further Examples
docs.text:
The same workflow applies to the other certified training methods: choose the corresponding model wrapper and configure its method-specific hyperparameters. For example, the expressive losses combine adversarial and IBP objectives, while CC-Dist additionally uses a pretrained teacher.

The following tutorials demonstrate CTRAIN's functionality in more detail:

  • Certified training: Loading MNIST, configuring a wrapper, training and saving weights.
  • Model evaluation: Loading the training example's weights and evaluating natural, certified and adversarial accuracy.
  • Hyperparameter optimisation: Searching for configurations and selecting models from their Pareto fronts.
  • General output properties: Training a small controller with bounded outputs over a declared input box.
  • ONNX and VNNLIB: Importing networks and specifications for training and repair.
  • MNIST arithmetic: Training predicted digit values and their sum with an affine consistency property.

The MNIST notebooks use real data. Run certified training before model evaluation, which loads its saved weights. The ONNX/VNNLIB notebook requires your own model and specification files. More detailed configuration and complete-verification workflows are covered in the guides.

docs.title: Development and Local Documentation
docs.text:
With the development and Git dependencies installed, run the CPU test suite from the repository root:

python -m pytest -q

The suite includes isolated notebook smoke checks with offline fixtures and reduced training budgets. Optional CUDA and complete-verifier checks are described in the repository's tests/README.md.

To view the documentation locally, start the MkDocs server from the same directory:

mkdocs serve

The documentation build renders the notebooks without executing their training or verification cells.

docs.title: Gaussian Loss Smoothing
docs.text:
Tighter bounding methods can provide more precise approximations of a network's reachable outputs, but the resulting training objectives may be difficult to optimise. Balauca et al. (2025), Gaussian Loss Smoothing Enables Certified Training with Tight Convex Relaxations, address this challenge by smoothing the loss over Gaussian perturbations of the network parameters. This enables certified training with tighter relaxations, such as those used by CROWN.

CTRAIN provides Gaussian loss smoothing through GLSModelWrapper, supporting Randomized Gradient Smoothing (RGS) and Policy Gradients with Parameter-based Exploration (PGPE). Both methods estimate updates using losses at perturbed parameter values. The resulting network is the centre model, which can be evaluated and verified through CTRAIN's common interfaces.

docs.title: Training Objective
docs.text:
Let theta denote the network parameters and L_bound the certified classification loss computed using the selected bounding method. Gaussian loss smoothing considers the expected loss under Gaussian parameter perturbations:

L_GLS(theta) = E_noise[L_bound(theta + noise)]

The parameter sigma controls the standard deviation of the Gaussian distribution. Since computing this expectation exactly is intractable, RGS and PGPE approximate the update using a finite collection of perturbed networks. The perturbations act on the model parameters; the input region remains the one specified by eps and the data loader.

docs.title: Randomized Gradient Smoothing
docs.text:
RGS computes ordinary gradients of the loss at independently sampled parameter values and averages them to update the centre model. It therefore requires gradients through the selected bound computation. The samples argument controls the number of sampled networks per optimiser step and defaults to two.

RGS uses a fixed noise scale, which can optionally be reduced during training through sigma_decay_milestones and sigma_decay_factor. It is the first-order approximation studied in the paper; for discontinuous objectives, averaging sampled gradients need not give an unbiased gradient of the Gaussian-smoothed loss.

docs.title: Policy Gradients with Parameter-based Exploration
docs.text:
PGPE estimates updates from loss values at mirrored parameter perturbations, evaluating both theta + noise and theta - noise. It updates the centre parameters and learns a separate Gaussian standard deviation for each parameter, using an additional centre-loss evaluation as a baseline for the scale updates. Thus, its update does not require backpropagating through the certified loss.

For PGPE, samples must be a positive even integer, counting the perturbed loss evaluations in the mirrored pairs. The centre-loss baseline is evaluated in addition to these samples. The sigma argument provides the initial standard deviation and sigma_lr controls its learning rate. CTRAIN limits each scale change to 2% per update.

docs.title: Training with CTRAIN
docs.text:
In the following example, we train a CNN on CIFAR-10 using RGS with CROWN bounds, for robustness against ℓ∞ perturbations with radius ε = 2/255. First, we import the required functions and load the dataset using CTRAIN. The loader supplies the normalisation metadata and input limits required for bound propagation.

from CTRAIN.data_loaders import load_cifar10
from CTRAIN.model_definitions import CNN_GLS
from CTRAIN.model_wrappers import GLSModelWrapper

input_shape = (3, 32, 32)
train_loader, test_loader = load_cifar10(batch_size=128, val_split=False)
model = CNN_GLS(in_shape=input_shape, depth=5, width=16)

CNN_GLS provides the architectures used in the GLS paper. Here, depth=5 and width=16 select CNN5, without BatchNorm or an embedded normalisation layer. Input normalisation is handled by the data loader.

docs.title: Configuring and Training the Wrapper
docs.text:
Now, we wrap the network with GLSModelWrapper. We choose two RGS samples per update, an initial noise scale of 1e-3, and CROWN for the certified loss. The wrapper uses Adam by default; here, we explicitly set its learning rate to 5e-5.

We configure one warm-up epoch on clean cross-entropy, followed by 80 ramp-up epochs during which the perturbation radius increases linearly to its target. Training then continues at the full radius. We reduce both the learning rate and the RGS noise scale at epochs 120 and 140, using separate decay factors for the two schedules.

wrapped_model = GLSModelWrapper(
    model=model,
    input_shape=input_shape,
    eps=2 / 255,
    num_epochs=160,
    estimator="rgs",
    samples=2,
    sigma=1e-3,
    bound_method="CROWN",
    lr=5e-5,
    warm_up_epochs=1,
    ramp_up_epochs=80,
    lr_decay_kwargs={"milestones": (120, 140), "gamma": 0.2},
    sigma_decay_milestones=(120, 140),
    sigma_decay_factor=0.4,
    device="cuda",
)
wrapped_model.train_model(train_loader)

The bound_method option supports "IBP", "CROWN-IBP" and "CROWN", using CTRAIN's existing auto_LiRPA bound computations. CROWN-IBP uses IBP for intermediate bounds, while CROWN uses linear relaxations throughout. The default adaptive ReLU relaxation used by CROWN corresponds to DeepPoly.

docs.title: Using PGPE
docs.text:
To use PGPE, select estimator="pgpe", choose an even samples value and configure the scale learning rate through sigma_lr. Omit sigma_decay_milestones, since PGPE learns its scales during optimisation. The main configuration differences are:

Option RGS PGPE samples Number of independent gradient samples Number of perturbed loss evaluations, in mirrored pairs sigma Fixed standard deviation, with optional scheduled decay Initial standard deviation for learned parameterwise scales sigma_lr Unused Learning rate for the scales sigma_decay_milestones Epochs at which the fixed scale is reduced Must be empty

The paper's PGPE experiments start from adversarially pretrained models. To fine-tune such a model in CTRAIN, load its native PyTorch weights before constructing the wrapper and set shi_init=False to preserve the initial weights.

docs.title: Evaluating the Model
docs.text:
Finally, we set the model to evaluation mode and assess its natural, certified and adversarial accuracy using the common evaluation interface:

wrapped_model.eval()
std_acc, cert_acc, adv_acc = wrapped_model.evaluate(test_loader, eval_method="CROWN")

Evaluation uses the centre network with sound bounds over the full nominal input box. Complete verification is available through wrapped_model.evaluate_complete, using α,β-CROWN or NeuralSAT. The evaluation guide explains the available methods and interpretation of results.

docs.title: Training Behaviour and Configuration
docs.text:
Shi initialisation is enabled by default. Shi regularisation and L1 regularisation are optional and both default to zero. The trainer uses clean cross-entropy during warm-up and certified cross-entropy at positive perturbation radii, with the configured regularisers added to the objective. Gaussian parameter sampling applies during both phases.

Sampled parameters and buffers are restored between evaluations and on failure. For models with BatchNorm, running buffers update once per training batch at the centre model. Optional population recalibration is available through population_bn. If gradient_clip is set, RGS clips each sampled gradient before averaging, while PGPE clips the estimated centre gradient. Further shared options are described in the training guide.

Without a validation loader, train_model returns the final weights. Supplying val_loader enables selection by the centre model's certified validation accuracy after ramp-up, at the configured evaluation radius and using the selected bounding method. Trajectory checkpoints retain the centre and scale optimiser states, the Gaussian scales and the learning-rate scheduler. Recreate the same estimator and sample count when resuming; the checkpoint guide explains saving and restoration.

docs.title: Hyperparameter Optimisation
docs.text:
GLS supports the shared hyperparameter optimisation interface, including multi-objective searches over natural and certified validation accuracy. The search space contains the shared training parameters and the initial Gaussian scale sigma, searched logarithmically over [1e-5, 1e-2] with default 1e-3.

The estimator, sample count, bound method and remaining GLS options are preserved when the wrapper is recreated for each trial. Thus, choose these settings when constructing the wrapper and use separate validation data to investigate the remaining training parameters.

docs.title: Implementation and API Reference
docs.text:
CTRAIN implements the RGS and PGPE update procedures using its existing certified losses and bound computations. Parameter samples are evaluated sequentially within the trainer. When translating PGPE configurations from the released implementation, note that its popsize counts mirrored pairs; the corresponding CTRAIN setting is samples=2 * popsize.

The implemented training bounds are IBP, CROWN-IBP and CROWN. HBox and the paper's one-step optimised α-CROWN training variant are outside the current wrapper's scope. The example above demonstrates the library workflow; reproducing reported accuracies additionally requires matching the experiment's architecture, initialisation, preprocessing, training configuration and verification protocol.

The API reference documents the GLS wrapper, trainer and optimiser, and the underlying IBP and CROWN/CROWN-IBP bound computations.

docs.title: Interval Bound Propagation
docs.text:
Interval Bound Propagation (IBP) is a computationally efficient approach to certified training. It propagates lower and upper activation bounds through a network using interval arithmetic, obtaining a sound enclosure of the reachable outputs for a given input region. These bounds can then be used to construct a certified training loss, as demonstrated by Gowal et al. (2018).

CTRAIN provides IBP training through ShiIBPModelWrapper, incorporating the initialisation and regularisation improvements proposed by Shi et al. (2021), Fast Certified Robust Training with Short Warmup. These improvements address excessively wide initial bounds and imbalanced ReLU activation states, helping stabilise certified training.

docs.title: Training Objective
docs.text:
For each input, CTRAIN constructs a perturbation box and clips it to the feasible input limits. IBP propagates this region through the network to compute lower bounds on the classification margins, which are the differences between the correct-class logit and each competing logit.

Cross-entropy evaluated from these lower margin bounds gives an upper bound on the worst-case classification loss over the input box. If every lower margin bound is positive, the network correctly classifies the input throughout that region. A non-positive bound leaves the property unresolved by IBP; tighter verification methods may still establish robustness.

At positive perturbation radii, the trainer supports a scheduled combination of clean and IBP losses:

L_train = kappa * L_clean + (1 - kappa) * L_IBP

The start_kappa and end_kappa arguments specify the clean-loss weights at the start and end of ramp-up. Both default to zero, giving the IBP classification objective during positive-radius training. At zero radius, the trainer uses clean cross-entropy. Configured Shi and L1 regularisers are added separately.

docs.title: Training with CTRAIN
docs.text:
In the following example, we train CNN7 on CIFAR-10 for robustness against ℓ∞ perturbations with radius ε = 2/255. First, we import the required functions, load the dataset and construct the model.

from CTRAIN.data_loaders import load_cifar10
from CTRAIN.model_definitions import CNN7_Shi
from CTRAIN.model_wrappers import ShiIBPModelWrapper

input_shape = (3, 32, 32)
train_loader, test_loader = load_cifar10(batch_size=128, val_split=False)
model = CNN7_Shi(in_shape=input_shape)

The loader supplies normalisation metadata and input limits. Thus, the wrapper accepts eps in raw pixel units and constructs the appropriate regions for the normalised inputs. See the data and models guide for custom data-loading workflows.

docs.title: Configuring and Training the Wrapper
docs.text:
Now, we wrap the network with ShiIBPModelWrapper. We configure one warm-up epoch using clean cross-entropy, followed by 80 ramp-up epochs during which the perturbation radius gradually increases to its target. Training then continues at the full radius. The learning rate is reduced by a factor of 0.2 at epochs 120 and 140.

wrapped_model = ShiIBPModelWrapper(
    model=model,
    input_shape=input_shape,
    eps=2 / 255,
    num_epochs=160,
    warm_up_epochs=1,
    ramp_up_epochs=80,
    lr_decay_kwargs={"milestones": (120, 140), "gamma": 0.2},
    device="cuda",
)
wrapped_model.train_model(train_loader)

The wrapper delegates to the library trainer, which applies Shi initialisation when starting from epoch zero and manages the schedules, regularisation, optimisation and checkpoints. The underlying PyTorch architecture remains available through wrapped_model.original_model.

docs.title: Evaluating the Model
docs.text:
Finally, we set the model to evaluation mode and assess its natural, certified and adversarial accuracy. The following call uses IBP for certification and PGD for adversarial evaluation:

wrapped_model.eval()
std_acc, cert_acc, adv_acc = wrapped_model.evaluate(test_loader, eval_method="IBP")

Other supported evaluation methods include CROWN-IBP, CROWN and α-CROWN. Complete verification through α,β-CROWN or NeuralSAT is available via evaluate_complete. These choices concern post-training evaluation and can be selected independently of the training method.

docs.title: Training Behaviour and Configuration
docs.text:
The shi_reg_weight option controls the regularisers that encourage bound tightness and balanced ReLU activation states during warm-up and ramp-up. It defaults to 0.5; shi_reg_decay=True reduces their contribution as the perturbation radius grows. L1 regularisation is controlled separately through l1_reg_weight, which defaults to 1e-6.

The train_eps_factor scales the target training radius, while evaluation continues to use the nominal eps. Optional population BatchNorm recalibration is available through population_bn, which defaults to False. When enabled, recalibration uses training data after each epoch, before validation selection and checkpointing. Further shared options are described in the training guide.

Without a validation loader, train_model returns the final weights. Supplying val_loader enables selection after ramp-up by the smallest configured validation data loss at the evaluation radius. With the default zero clean-loss weight, this is the IBP validation loss. The checkpoint guide explains saving and resumption, including the distinction between selected inference weights and training trajectories.

docs.title: Hyperparameter Optimisation
docs.text:
The wrapper supports the shared hyperparameter optimisation interface, including multi-objective searches over natural and certified validation accuracy. Its configuration space includes the training schedules, optimiser settings, regularisation weights, training-radius factor and clean-loss mixing coefficients.

Reserve separate validation data for the search and use the test split to assess the selected model. The hyperparameter optimisation tutorial demonstrates how to obtain and select models from a Pareto front.

docs.title: Implementation and API Reference
docs.text:
The wrapper delegates to shi_train_model, while the IBP loss and bound functions own the margin and interval computations. Bound propagation uses auto_LiRPA. CROWN-IBP extends the training workflow with a backward linear-relaxation bound and has its own method page.

The example above demonstrates the library workflow; reproducing published accuracies additionally requires matching the architecture, preprocessing, schedules, regularisation and evaluation protocol.

The API reference documents the Shi-IBP wrapper, trainer, loss, IBP bounds, initialisation and Shi regularisers.

docs.title: IBP-R
docs.text:
IBP-R augments adversarial training with an IBP-based regulariser that encourages tighter approximations of the network's ReLU activations. Proposed by De Palma et al. (2022), IBP Regularization for Verified Adversarial Robustness via Branch-and-Bound, the method combines adversarial attacks over enlarged input regions with a penalty on the areas of convex ReLU relaxations. This encourages networks that retain the predictive performance of adversarial training while facilitating subsequent verification.

CTRAIN provides IBP-R through IBPRModelWrapper, reusing the library's PGD attack and auto_LiRPA interval propagation. The wrapper configures the training radius, attack and regularisation parameters, while the trainer owns the schedules, optimisation and model selection.

docs.title: Training Objective
docs.text:
IBP-R uses PGD to obtain adversarial examples and IBP to compute pre-activation bounds at each ReLU. When a ReLU's interval crosses zero, its convex relaxation introduces a triangular approximation region. For lower and upper pre-activation bounds, the area is:

area = relu(-lower) * relu(upper) / 2

Stable ReLUs contribute zero area. CTRAIN sums these areas over all neurons and ReLU layers, then averages over the batch. The coefficient rho weights this penalty in the objective. Since the area already includes the factor 1 / 2, a paper-table entry of rho / 2 = 1e-4 corresponds to rho=2e-4 in the wrapper.

During ramp-up, the trainer increases both the perturbation radius and an adversarial mixing weight kappa linearly from zero to their targets. The classification and area terms are combined as follows:

L_train = (1 - kappa) * L_clean + kappa * (L_adv + rho * R)

Here, L_clean and L_adv are the clean and adversarial cross-entropy losses, and R is the batch-mean ReLU area penalty. Once kappa reaches one, training uses adversarial cross-entropy plus the area penalty. Configured L1 and Shi regularisation are added separately by the trainer.

docs.title: Regularisation Masking
docs.text: With regularisation_mask=True, the area penalty includes only samples whose adversarial predictions are correct. The denominator remains the original batch size, so masking removes contributions without renormalising over the retained samples. The classification loss still uses all samples. Masking defaults to False.

docs.title: Training with CTRAIN
docs.text:
In the following example, we train the CNN7 architecture proposed by Shi et al. on CIFAR-10 for robustness against ℓ∞ perturbations with radius ε = 2/255. First, we import the required functions, load the dataset and construct the model.

from CTRAIN.data_loaders import load_cifar10
from CTRAIN.model_definitions import CNN7_Shi
from CTRAIN.model_wrappers import IBPRModelWrapper

input_shape = (3, 32, 32)
train_loader, test_loader = load_cifar10(batch_size=100, val_split=False)
model = CNN7_Shi(in_shape=input_shape)

We use CNN7 here to demonstrate the common wrapper interface. The original study used smaller five-layer and four-layer networks at 2/255 and 8/255, respectively.

Now, we wrap the model with IBPRModelWrapper. The train_eps_factor corresponds to the paper's radius multiplier α: it enlarges both the training IBP region and the input-attack region. Here, train_eps_factor=2.1 gives a target training radius of 4.2/255, while evaluation continues to use the nominal radius of 2/255.

We configure 800 epochs, including 600 ramp-up epochs. The wrapper uses SGD by default, with an initial learning rate of 0.01 and exponential decay by a factor of 0.95. In this example, we delay decay until after ramp-up and disable CTRAIN's additional Shi initialisation and regularisation to retain the original IBP-R objective.

wrapped_model = IBPRModelWrapper(
    model=model,
    input_shape=input_shape,
    eps=2 / 255,
    num_epochs=800,
    warm_up_epochs=0,
    ramp_up_epochs=600,
    train_eps_factor=2.1,
    rho=2e-4,
    regularisation_mask=False,
    lr=0.01,
    lr_decay_kwargs={"gamma": 0.95},
    lr_decay_after_ramp_up=True,
    l1_reg_weight=2e-5,
    pgd_steps=8,
    pgd_alpha=0.25,
    shi_init=False,
    shi_reg_weight=0,
    device="cuda",
)
wrapped_model.train_model(train_loader)

The loader supplies the normalisation metadata and input limits, so radii are specified in raw pixel units and the resulting regions are clipped to feasible inputs. Data loading and custom preprocessing are described in the data and models guide.

docs.title: Evaluating the Model
docs.text:
Finally, we set the model to evaluation mode and assess its natural, certified and adversarial accuracy. The following call uses CROWN for incomplete verification and PGD for adversarial evaluation at the original eps:

wrapped_model.eval()
std_acc, cert_acc, adv_acc = wrapped_model.evaluate(test_loader, eval_method="CROWN")

Complete verification is available through wrapped_model.evaluate_complete, using α,β-CROWN or NeuralSAT. The area penalty encourages verifiability during training; certificates are obtained separately over the full nominal input region. See the evaluation guide for the available methods and solver settings.

docs.title: Training Behaviour and Configuration
docs.text:
The train_eps_factor must be finite and at least one. The separate pgd_eps_factor optionally scales only the attack search range, leaving the training IBP region unchanged. The pgd_steps, pgd_alpha and pgd_restarts arguments configure the attack; step-size decay is controlled through pgd_decay_milestones and pgd_alpha_decay_factor.

CTRAIN runs attacks in evaluation mode and evaluates the resulting adversarial points and bounds in the caller's training mode. PGD step sizes use CTRAIN's maximum clipped half-width scaling, and the area penalty is computed from fresh IBP intervals for the current batch.

By default, CTRAIN enables Shi initialisation and adds Shi regularisation during warm-up and ramp-up with shi_reg_weight=0.5 and shi_reg_decay=True. The example disables these additions explicitly. Similarly, lr_decay_after_ramp_up defaults to False, so delayed decay must be requested when following the paper's schedule. Gradient clipping defaults to 10.

Optional population BatchNorm recalibration is available through population_bn. The relu_upper_retention option defaults to 1.0; values below one produce an unsound training surrogate and are not used for ordinary certification. Further shared settings are described in the training guide.

Without a validation loader, train_model returns the final weights. Supplying val_loader enables selection by adversarial validation accuracy after ramp-up, at the original evaluation radius. This is an empirical selection metric. The trainer recalibrates BatchNorm, when requested, before selection and checkpointing. The checkpoint guide explains trajectory saving and resumption, including the distinction from selected inference weights.

docs.title: Translating Published Configurations
docs.text:
Figure 5 in Appendix F.1 of the paper's second version reports separate configurations for the two CIFAR-10 radii and for masked and unmasked regularisation. The corresponding CTRAIN settings are:

Radius Batch size train_eps_factor rho l1_reg_weight regularisation_mask 2/255 100 2.1 2e-4 2e-5 False or True 8/255, unmasked 150 1.7 0.01 1e-5 False 8/255, masked 150 1.6 0.02 1e-5 True

The authors' released README contains a different 8/255 command: it enables masking but uses a radius factor of 1.7 and rho / 2 = 0.005, corresponding to rho=0.01. This is a distinct configuration from the masked Figure 5 setting and should be kept separate when comparing experiments.

docs.title: Hyperparameter Optimisation
docs.text:
IBP-R supports the shared hyperparameter optimisation interface, including multi-objective searches over natural and certified validation accuracy. Its search space includes the shared training parameters, rho, regularisation masking and PGD settings. The training-radius factor is searched over [1, 3], and rho logarithmically over [1e-6, 0.1], using the configuration key ibp_r:rho.

SGD is the default optimiser for this search, with Adam, AdamW and RAdam also available. HPO trials use CTRAIN's shared milestone-based learning-rate schedule; the exponential schedule in the example applies to direct wrapper training. Fixed BatchNorm, ReLU-retention, Shi-initialisation and PGD-decay options are retained when recreating trial wrappers. Reserve separate validation data for the search and use the test split to assess the selected model.

docs.title: Implementation and API Reference
docs.text:
CTRAIN implements equation (6) and the optional regularisation mask from Section 3 of the paper using PyTorch and auto_LiRPA. The authors' implementation uses JAX. When comparing results, account for differences in attack bookkeeping, step-size scaling, BatchNorm policy, initialisation and L1 regularisation; CTRAIN's L1 helper regularises linear and convolutional weights.

The paper also introduces UPB branching and uses the OVAL verification framework. These are outside the training wrapper's scope; post-training verification uses CTRAIN's existing backends. The example above demonstrates the library workflow, and a matching configuration alone does not establish reproduction of reported accuracies.

The API reference documents the IBP-R wrapper, trainer, loss and area penalty and underlying IBP bounds.

docs.title: General Input-Output Properties
docs.text:
Beyond local robustness for image classification, CTRAIN supports training against more general input-output specifications. These include output-range constraints, safety conditions for controllers and relations between multiple predictions. Users supply a task loss and a collection of specifications, each consisting of closed input boxes and an output property expressed as a finite Boolean combination of affine inequalities.

For a network to satisfy a specification, its output property must hold for every input in every declared box. CTRAIN formulates these requirements through satisfaction margins, analogous to the classification margins used for local robustness. This allows existing certified training methods to be adapted to more general specifications while retaining a common interface for training and verification.

CTRAIN provides this workflow through PropertyModelWrapper. The wrapper combines the supplied task loss with a property objective, delegates optimisation to the property trainer and exposes fresh certification over the declared domains.

docs.title: Training Objective
docs.text:
For network output y, an affine comparison a(y) >= b(y) has satisfaction margin a(y) - b(y). Conjunction takes the minimum of its constituent margins, while disjunction takes their maximum:

m(a >= b) = a(y) - b(y)
m(And(phi, psi)) = min(m(phi), m(psi))
m(Or(phi, psi)) = max(m(phi), m(psi))

A positive margin therefore implies satisfaction of the formula. CTRAIN appends the operations required to compute these margins to the network and uses auto_LiRPA to obtain lower bounds over each input box. Outer conjunctions are split into separate requirements, while nested disjunctions retain their logical structure.

At each optimisation step, the trainer samples K property boxes independently of the task examples. With the default hinge objective, it combines the task loss with the sum of lower-margin deficits:

L_train = L_task + (lambda / K) * sum_k sum_j max(0, delta - lower_margin[k, j])

Here, lambda is controlled by property_weight, and delta by margin. Each property penalty vanishes once its lower bound reaches the positive target margin. This avoids encouraging further increases in satisfaction margins that may come at the expense of task performance. The target margin is distinct from the logical satisfaction threshold of zero.

docs.title: Training with CTRAIN
docs.text:
In the following example, we train a small controller whose two actions should remain within [-0.1, 0.1] for every state in a declared box. The task loss encourages the controller to match a proportional control law.
